newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 17.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BID ACTIVITY IS STIFLED BY ELECTION UNCERTAINTY

Despite the recent spate of takeovers, bid activity is declining in the run-up to the general election. Approaches to the Office of Fair Trading by companies wanting advice on whether bids could be referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission have slowed to a trickle. Although still receiving inquires about modest bids, an insider said there was nothing in the pipeline to suggest a major takeover was in the offing.
-- INVESTCORP MAKES RECORD 90 MILLION DOLLAR PROFIT

The Bahrain-based investment group Investcorp reported record profits yesterday of US$90.4 million. Despite currently having no UK holdings, it was revealed last week that Investcorp is financing a 400-millio-pound-stg bid for Welcome Break. Last year the group distributed $1.1 billion. Of the record profits, $30 million will be paid in dividends.
-- SUMITOMO COPPER TRADER GOES ON TRIAL

Yasuo Hamanaka, the former Sumitomo copper trader blamed for running up losses of 1.6 billion pounds stg, went on trial today in Tokyo for fraud and forgery. Mr Hamanaka could be jailed for up to 15 years if found guilty of all charges. He is the only person who has been arrested in the scandal although a global investigation is under way.
THE TIMES
-- TELECOMS PACT SIGNALS END OF MONOPOLIES

An international agreement signed at the weekend will end most government and major private telecom monopolies. The agreement to deregulate telecommunications markets could add 625 billion pounds stg, or four percent, to the value of global economic output over the next 10 years. The agreement comes into force from 1998 and should ultimately benefit the consumer. The World Trade Organisation, which supervised the Geneva negotiations, predicted the creation of thousands of jobs as well as reduced phone costs.
-- UNION OFFERS NEW PLAN TO TRANSFORM THE POST OFFICE

According to new proposals from the Post Office's main trade union, the Post Office should be transformed into an independent public sector company to give it greater commercial freedom. The Communication Workers' Union argues that it should be possible for the Post Office to stay in public ownership and have greater commercial freedom through a interlocking package of measures.
-- DEMERGED BRITISH GAS WELCOMES DAWN OF A NEW ERA
British Gas will split in two this morning and official trading will begin in BG, the renamed British Gas shares, and Centrica, the demerged gas supply business.
Small shareholders, of which there are about 1.7 million, will receive one Centrica share for every British Gas share they hold.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BILLION-DOLLAR NORTH SEA OIL PROJECT

South Korea's state-owned oil company, Pedeco, is planning to invest US$1 billion in British North Sea oilfields over the next three years. Pedeco want to develop and operate North Sea fields and is in talks with unidentified UK and US groups about participating in the 17th round of North Sea licensing. The move is part of a long-term strategy to build up oil reserves as a buffer against oil price increases.
-- INDUSTRY FIGURES BOLSTER CLARKE'S RATES STANCE

Confederation of British Industry figures show pay rates in manufacturing are flat and suggest no head of steam is building among manufacturers for large pay rises. The government will use the figures as another indication that inflationary pressures remain subdued and underpin Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's decision not to raise interest rates before the general election.
-- GUS FREES 900 MILLION POUNDS ASSET

The UK's largest mail order group, Great Universal Stores is thought to be planning a joint venture to exploit the potential of its property bank. Negotiations are believed taking place between GUS and property company British Land to transfer part of its 900-million-stg property portfolio to an off-balance sheet vehicle managed by British Land.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- PEARSON BACKS EX-PENGUIN BOSS AHEAD OF GRILLING

The Pearson board is backing the former head of Penguin Books in America, Peter Mayer, believing that he had no knowledge of the accounting scandal that has forced the media group to take a 100-million-stg charge against its 1996 accounts. Mr Mayer will be interviewed by Pearson today.
-- FATE OF SINGLE CURRENCY HANGS IN THE BALANCE

According to a new report from the London Business School, the success of failure of a single currency will depend on decisions made over the coming year. The report, commissioned by the Economist Intelligence Unit, is the most extensive and balanced so far on the pros and cons of the single currency project. It says the EMU does not condemn Europe to failure or guarantee its success, and the same is true for abandoning the project. Everything will depend on the wisdom of the choices that governments still have to make.
-- UTILITIES 'COMPLACENT' OVER 2000 CRISIS

Taskforce 2000, the body set up by the Department of Trade and Industry to publicise the millennium problem, has criticised the heads of the private utilities for being complacent over preparations for the looming year-2000 computer crisis. Industry experts have predicted chaos across the world as computer systems shut themselves down when the date changes.
